subject: Physiology
topic: Red Blood Cell Characteristics and Functions
subtopic: Erythrocyte physiology, oxygen transport and carbon dioxide transport
concept: Red blood cells are specialized, flexible, anucleate cells whose principal physiological role is transporting oxygen and contributing to carbon dioxide transport and acid-base homeostasis.

content.definition: An erythrocyte is a mature red blood cell specialized for respiratory gas transport. Its high hemoglobin content and flexible biconcave form allow efficient oxygen loading in the lungs, oxygen unloading in tissues and participation in carbon dioxide transport.
content.explanation: Mature human RBCs lack a nucleus and mitochondria and therefore do not consume the oxygen they transport through oxidative phosphorylation. They obtain ATP mainly through anaerobic glycolysis. Their biconcave shape provides a high surface-area-to-volume ratio and supports deformation through small vessels. A typical RBC circulates for about 120 days before senescent cells are removed mainly by macrophages in the spleen and liver.
content.mechanism: Oxygen binds reversibly to the iron-containing heme groups of hemoglobin. About 98% of transported oxygen is carried bound to hemoglobin, with a small fraction dissolved in plasma. Oxygen loading is favored in the lungs, while tissue conditions promote unloading. Increased temperature, increased carbon dioxide, decreased pH and increased 2,3-BPG decrease hemoglobin oxygen affinity and shift the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, facilitating oxygen unloading. RBCs also participate in carbon dioxide transport: carbon dioxide enters RBCs, carbonic anhydrase catalyzes conversion with water to carbonic acid, and much of the resulting bicarbonate is transported in plasma. Hemoglobin also buffers hydrogen ions and thereby contributes to acid-base balance.
content.structure: Mature RBCs are flexible biconcave discs approximately 6–8 micrometers in diameter. They contain a plasma membrane supported by a spectrin-based cytoskeleton and are densely packed with hemoglobin. They lack a nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes and endoplasmic reticulum.
content.function: RBCs transport oxygen from lungs to tissues, participate in carbon dioxide transport from tissues to lungs, buffer hydrogen ions and contribute to blood viscosity and rheological behavior.
content.clinical_relevance: Reduced RBC number or hemoglobin concentration can impair oxygen delivery and cause anemia. Abnormal hemoglobin structure or concentration can alter oxygen transport. Changes in RBC deformability, membrane integrity or lifespan can contribute to hemolytic and other blood disorders.
content.diagnosis: RBC physiology is assessed clinically using hemoglobin concentration, hematocrit, RBC count and red-cell indices, together with peripheral smear and reticulocyte count when indicated.
content.treatment: Management depends on the underlying disorder affecting RBC production, hemoglobin, membrane function, destruction or blood loss.
